strengths: Novel theoretical contributions: Theorem 3.2 rigorously proves block-level factorization reduces NELBO vs. token-wise independence, with formal quantification of the improvement. Theorem 3.3 establishes necessity/sufficiency of soft-conditioning and demonstrates top-k truncation can exclude the global mode.

Well-motivated practical solution: Clearly articulates the coherence problem in parallel DLM sampling and proposes a method that maintains key DLM capabilities (bidirectionality, infilling, self-correction) unlike prior quasi-AR approaches.

Clever soft-conditioning design: Projecting marginals into AR embedding space elegantly bridges DLM's rich information with AR model's representational space. Table 1 ablation convincingly shows soft-conditioning is essential (e.g., 68.9→55.5% accuracy drop with hard-conditioning).

Solid experimental validation on code generation: Comprehensive benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, BigCodeBench plus EvalPlus), both static/dynamic parallelism, establishes new Pareto frontier for accuracy vs. latency with 2× speedup maintaining base model accuracy.

Thorough experimental documentation: Detailed experimental setup in Appendix A including tokenizer alignment, special tokens, and extraction logic enables reproducibility. Clear figures effectively illustrate the method.
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: Experiments only on code generation with a single base model (Dream-Coder-7B). Despite the title/abstract suggesting a general DLM method, generalization to other domains, models, and tasks is completely unvalidated. This critically limits impact claims for a method positioned as advancing DLM decoding broadly.

Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 3.2 predicts larger blocks reduce NELBO (confirmed by Figure 3 training loss), but Figure 4 shows sharp inference degradation at large B (B=8: 29.9% vs B=2: 68.9% on HumanEval). This suggests practical benefits come from the auxiliary AR model rather than block-level diffusion itself, undermining the theoretical motivation.

Artificial generation constraints: Section 3.5 introduces 'candidate scoping' limiting unmasking to 10 blocks to prevent premature EOS prediction. This ad-hoc workaround suggests fundamental instability issues. Table 2 shows extending scope to 50 blocks maintains throughput but drops accuracy significantly, raising questions about the method's robustness.

Incomplete experimental comparisons: No comparison with recent methods (discrete copula diffusion cited but not compared). ADJUST baseline appears weak but comparison unfair given different design goals. No ablation isolating contributions of block-level diffusion vs. auxiliary AR model vs. soft-conditioning alone.

Limited analysis of what the auxiliary model learns: No investigation of which coherence error types are fixed, what the AR model actually learns beyond basic denoising, or how performance varies with vocabulary size and task differences. Soft-conditioning contribution feels somewhat orthogonal to the block-diffusion narrative.

strengths: Strong theoretical contributions: Theorem 3.2 formally proves block-based factorization reduces NELBO with explicit quantification of gains; Theorem 3.3 elegantly justifies soft-conditioning necessity with counterexample to top-k truncation.
Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of conditional token independence bias in parallel DLM decoding, supported by compelling examples (Figure 1).
Elegant soft-conditioning interface (Eq. 4) that enables leveraging pretrained AR models without extensive retraining by projecting marginals into embedding space.
Comprehensive code generation evaluation across multiple benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, BigCodeBench) with substantial practical improvements (56pp syntax error reduction, new Pareto frontier).
Extensive ablations validating design choices: conditioning strategy, AR model size, scope, generation order, and batch sizes. Demonstrates larger AR models don't improve performance.
Preserves non-causal DLM capabilities (infilling, planning) while enabling parallel generation—important differentiator from AR-only approaches.
Reproducibility: detailed experimental setup, promised code release, fixed seeds, single-GPU evaluation with specified hardware and hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: only tested on code generation with single base model (Dream-Coder-7B). No evaluation on natural language generation, summarization, or other domains. Generalizability claims lack support for a general ML venue.

Throughput overhead at batch size 1 (61.4 vs 74.6 TPS, ~15-20% penalty) is non-negligible for latency-critical scenarios where DLMs are motivated, though amortized at batch size 8. Insufficient exploration of reducing overhead.

Incomplete baseline comparisons: only ADJUST compared empirically despite discussing APD, FlashDLLM, TiDAR in related work. Base DLM 'top-K' baseline is somewhat weak; stronger entropy-based or learned scheduling baselines missing.

Block size constrained to B≤8 due to sequential AR overhead, limiting parallelism potential (2-8 tokens/step). Theorem 3.2 suggests larger blocks are theoretically better, but practical constraints prevent realization. Limited exploration of solutions.

Training cost and generalization underspecified: AR trained on only 32k steps (6.7% of 4.48M examples), separate models needed for each block size, generalization across AR architectures unclear. No training time or computational cost analysis provided.

Non-causal capability preservation incompletely evaluated: infilling shows only 1.3-1.5× speedup vs 2-8× for code generation. ParallelBench and Graph Traversal use AR as verifier rather than direct generator, complicating assessment of truly preserved non-causal performance.

Soft-conditioning mechanism lacks deeper justification: why expected embeddings optimal over alternatives? Boundary tokens feel ad-hoc. Theorem 3.3 proves sufficiency of full marginals but not why expected embeddings optimally encode them.
Limited failure mode analysis: no error analysis, qualitative examples of remaining incoherence, or characterization of hard cases. Unclear which code structures still cause problems.

Design choices underspecified: 10-block lookahead default unexplained (Table 5 shows extending to 50 blocks has negligible throughput impact); entropy thresholds for dynamic parallelism lack sensitivity analysis; EOS penalty strategy appears heuristic.
